title: 2026 Law Student Pulse Survey: How Law Students Understand AI Better than Their Institutions
author: Thomson Reuters Institute

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Judgment development: AI exposure is not professional readiness
st.an: The source accepts that frequent AI use, confidence and perceived importance do not establish independent legal judgment. It materially develops the proposition by advocating supervised, ethically grounded integration, context-specific permissions and assessments that test AI fluency alongside foundational skills, while also assigning schools, employers and professional bodies responsibility for replacing threatened junior-development pathways. Its survey findings establish reported behaviour and attitudes, whereas its pipeline warnings remain predictions.
qs: Yet, those                           concerns do not argue against structured AI integration, rather they argue for it.

st.t: Law-firm pyramid: Efficiency threatens revenue and training
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s core claim that automating junior work threatens the expertise pipeline unless training is redesigned. It materially extends the synthesis with student-expectation evidence and specific institutional measures, especially supervised AI education, replacement developmental pathways and published employer competency standards. It does not establish profession-wide job contraction, because its employment evidence is primarily expectations and anecdote.
qs: As AI absorbs the tasks that historically taught                           early-career lawyers the basic mechanics of the legal practice, that developmental pathway through                           which the profession has reproduced its expertise appears to be eroding.
Firms should publish their AI competency expectations for incoming associates with the same                                     visibility and accountability they bring to pro bono targets.

st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s core framing of AI as supervised workflow augmentation rather than wholesale lawyer replacement, and materially extends its competence-risk thesis with a large student survey showing widespread self-directed use, weak institutional guidance and concern about erosion of entry-level development. It adds concrete proposals for structured, ethically grounded AI competency training and replacement developmental pathways, while appropriately treating employment effects as emerging risks rather than demonstrated profession-wide displacement.
qs: If AI absorbs entry-level work without a corresponding                           investment in the creation of new developmental pathways, the profession could face a skills deficit.

This can best                           be achieved by treating AI as a core professional competency on par with others — a learned skill that                           requires structured supervision and ethically grounded instruction.

st.t: Supervised AI: Verification may consume efficiency gains
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s supervised-aid model: AI can assist learning and legal work, but users must retain independent understanding and judgment. It materially extends the cluster by arguing that structured law-school instruction—rather than bans—is necessary to develop those capabilities before practice and prevent ungoverned, secret use.
qs: So, instead of focusing so much on whether                                 students are using AI, the conversation should be more about whether they                                 actually understand the material and can apply it on their own.

st.t: Task substitution: Complementarity can still reshape staffing
st.an: The source accepts that AI may substitute for entry-level legal tasks while lawyers retain judgment and supervisory roles, and materially develops the cluster by identifying a profession-wide apprenticeship and succession risk. It argues that staffing adaptation must include replacement developmental pathways and training in supervising AI, while acknowledging that its evidence is qualitative and predictive rather than measured.
qs: If AI absorbs entry-level work without a corresponding                           investment in the creation of new developmental pathways, the profession could face a skills deficit.

^GThe new jobs will be managing AI associates and providing the necessary                                   knowledge and discretion to nudge them in the right direction and                                   intervene when a mistake has been made.”                                                                                             — 2L who uses AI several times per week

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s core account of selective, supervised AI deployment and materially extends it into legal education and professional development. It provides survey-based evidence of fragmented preparation and argues for context-specific guidance, verification training and supervised integration, while developing the cluster’s junior-talent risk into a concrete call for replacement developmental pathways.
qs: They also argue for the                           kind of supervised, ethically grounded approach that transforms a genuine risk into a managed one.
If AI absorbs entry-level work without a corresponding                           investment in the creation of new developmental pathways, the profession could face a skills deficit.

st.t: AI curriculum: Assistance must preserve intellectual development
st.an: The source directly supports teaching AI-enabled legal practice while preserving independent skill development and professional judgment. It presents student perceptions—not measured learning outcomes—as evidence that AI competence and concern about over-reliance coexist, and it advocates core, context-specific instruction emphasizing accountability.
qs: Further, almost three-quarters (72%) say they agree that learning AI is an essential professional                           skill, and similar portion (74%) say believe that over-reliance on AI could cause them to struggle in                           developing critical legal skills.

Yet, to be the most ethically responsible, students need                           professional judgment that’s taught in an educational and practice ecosystem — and one that reinforces                           the risks and opportunities as well as students’ personal accountability when using these tools.

st.t: AI instruction: Timing divides educational reform
st.an: The survey supports developing independent legal judgment and AI competence together through structured, supervised, context-specific instruction. It rejects blanket bans and fragmented guidance while acknowledging that early over-reliance may impair foundational skills; its usage figures and student attitudes do not establish educational effectiveness.
qs: Further, almost three-quarters (72%) say they agree that learning AI is an essential professional                           skill, and similar portion (74%) say believe that over-reliance on AI could cause them to struggle in                           developing critical legal skills.

st.t: Associate training: Automation threatens expertise reproduction
st.an: The source directly supports the cluster’s central proposition: automating formative junior work risks weakening the future senior-lawyer pipeline unless firms create alternative developmental pathways. It also endorses training juniors in legal judgment and AI supervision, though its displacement and capability claims are forecasts and student testimony rather than measured outcomes.
qs: If AI absorbs entry-level work without a corresponding                           investment in the creation of new developmental pathways, the profession could face a skills deficit.

^GIt then becomes important to train entry level lawyers in how to develop                                   the needed skills to understand what’s good lawyering without necessarily                                   being subjected to the standard associate tasks that previously would                                   have given them these skills.

st.t: Law-school policy: Staged use bridges bans and adoption
st.an: The source aligns with the cluster’s central balance: law schools should preserve students’ independent understanding and judgment while teaching responsible AI use rather than imposing blanket bans. Its claims about concealed use and employer training burdens reinforce the rationale for supervised integration, but do not materially develop the cluster’s specific staged-instruction model.
qs: So, instead of focusing so much on whether                                 students are using AI, the conversation should be more about whether they                                 actually understand the material and can apply it on their own.

st.t: Legal workforce: Junior pipelines face the sharpest risk
st.an: The source directly supports the cluster’s central claim that the sharpest risk lies in the junior training and succession pipeline rather than wholesale replacement of senior lawyers. It identifies automation of formative entry-level work as the mechanism and makes the risk conditional on failure to create replacement developmental pathways; its displacement claims are student forecasts, not observed workforce evidence.
qs: If AI absorbs entry-level work without a corresponding                           investment in the creation of new developmental pathways, the profession could face a skills deficit.
Entry level tasks will be performed faster and                                   better by AI, but new lawyers still must be trained.

kp.k: Survey captures student perceptions, experiences, and expectations
kp.d: The white paper reports a web-based survey of 1,874 law students conducted April 6–19, 2026, combining quantitative questions with thematic analysis of 1,874 open-ended responses to Question 10. Respondents were 54% 1Ls, 26% 2Ls, 17% 3Ls, and 3% postgraduate law students. Its findings concern reported use and perceptions; its claims about future employment and skills development include student expectations and the Institute’s interpretations.
qs: a web-based survey of 1,874 law students conducted in April 2026.
Respondents included students enrolled in JD programs at the 1L (54%), 2L (26%), and 3L (17%) levels, as well as students pursuing postgraduate law degrees (3%).
thematic analysis of 1,874 open-ended responses to Question 10 informed the qualitative findings presented here.

kp.k: Students combine AI enthusiasm with concerns about foundational skills
kp.d: The survey reports that 72% regard learning AI as an essential professional skill and 74% believe over-reliance could impair critical legal skill development. The Institute interprets these attitudes as challenging institutional narratives that students are either reckless adopters or passive users unaware of AI’s risks, and argues that institutions should cultivate this balanced professional judgment.
qs: almost three-quarters (72%) say they agree that learning AI is an essential professional skill
Holding both positions simultaneously reflects a sophisticated understanding of what AI is and what it is not.

kp.k: Academic AI use is widespread and often self-taught
kp.d: More than half of respondents, 57%, report academic AI use several times weekly or more, rising to 84% among postgraduate students. The Institute attributes much of students’ understanding to self-education and personal experience rather than structured instruction. A quoted 1L describes AI as augmenting analysis and argument development rather than replacing thinking; this is a student account, not a measured learning outcome.
qs: More than half (57%) of students say they use AI several times a week or more for academic work, with 84% postgraduate students saying that.
Students have largely arrived at these conclusions without structured guidance, consistent institutional frameworks, or professionally supervised practice, the survey suggests.

When approached intentionally, AI functions as a tool that enhances analysis, exposes new ways of framing issues, and helps refine arguments. It does not replace critical thinking; it can strengthen it.

kp.k: Inconsistent institutional guidance leaves students feeling insufficiently prepared
kp.d: The survey finds that 48% report professor-specific AI policies, 15% report no institutional curriculum integration, and 32% disagree or strongly disagree that their school supplies the AI skills needed for their careers. Adequate preparation is reported by 36% of 1Ls and 30% of 3Ls. The Institute argues that practical exposure makes the divide between education and professional expectations increasingly visible.
qs: Almost half (48%) report that AI policies vary by professor
15% of law students say there is no curriculum integration whatsoever across their institution.
Among 1Ls, only 36% say they feel their school is preparing them adequately for AI in practice. Among 3Ls, that number drops to 30%.

kp.k: Students seek practical safeguards rather than binary risk warnings
kp.d: The qualitative findings identify demand for clear distinctions between permitted, encouraged, and prohibited uses across coursework, clinics, internships, and practice. Students recognize hallucinations, over-reliance, academic integrity ambiguities, and confidentiality risks, but seek instruction on managing them. The Institute recommends context-specific, supervised, ethically grounded training rather than treating responsible AI use as an isolated topic.
qs: Law students have independently identified the real risks, such as hallucinations, over-reliance, integrity gray zones, and confidentiality concerns.
The most repeated request from students is the establishment of a clear line between when and with what AI use is permitted, encouraged, and prohibited.
The conversation should not be ‘AI can hallucinate, so don’t use it,’ but rather ‘AI can hallucinate, so here’s what you need to do to guard against it.’

kp.k: Blanket bans can push AI use underground
kp.d: The Institute argues that bans or institutional silence sacrifice opportunities for supervised learning because AI is already embedded in academic life. Student comments describe privately shared study prompts and fear of cheating accusations. The source presents secrecy and reduced guidance as consequences of restrictive approaches, supported by qualitative accounts rather than a quantified comparison of school policies.
qs: When schools ban or ignore AI, they miss the opportunity to provide structured guidance, forcing the usage of AI tools underground.

The fear of being accused of cheating has pushed AI usage underground, which is the worst possible outcome for everyone. Underground usage means no quality control, no shared best practices, no institutional guidance, and no ethical framework.

kp.k: Students expect fewer entry-level roles and weaker professional formation
kp.d: Forty-seven percent expect entry-level positions to decrease as AI absorbs work. For impacts on early-career professionals over the next 2–3 years, Figure 3 reports net ratings, defined as positive minus negative percentages: overall impact −6; mentorship quality, learning through experience, and variety of career paths each −12; core skill development −14; independent judgment −31; and creation of AI qualifications +42. These are expectations, not observed employment or competence changes.
qs: 47% say they see entry-level positions decreasing as AI absorbs work
Impact of AI on early career professionals in the next 2-3 years
Base: 1874 and *NET = % Positive - % Negative.
The single exception is new AI proficiency qualifications, which receive a net positive rating of 42.

kp.k: Automating junior tasks could undermine future senior expertise
kp.d: The Institute warns conditionally that absorbing entry-level tasks without replacement developmental pathways could produce a future skills deficit and succession problems. It reports a student’s account of a large-firm partner saying effective AI tools had eliminated his practice group’s need for new associates for several years. Separately, a quoted 2L predicts AI will outperform associates on entry-level tasks and new lawyers will supervise AI work; these are anecdotal evidence and student predictions, respectively.
qs: A partner at a large law firm explained that his practice group had not needed to hire new associates for several years now because of how effective their AI tools had been.
If AI absorbs entry-level work without a corresponding investment in the creation of new developmental pathways, the profession could face a skills deficit.
The new jobs will be managing AI associates and providing the necessary knowledge and discretion to nudge them in the right direction and intervene when a mistake has been made.

kp.k: Employer expectations shift training responsibilities beyond law schools
kp.d: The Institute asserts that employers increasingly expect incoming lawyers to use AI appropriately and that inconsistent school preparation shifts training obligations to employers. It cites Fredrikson & Byron’s incorporation of AI fluency into associate development and anecdotal reports of firms asking summer associates about AI use during recruitment. It suggests employers may instead encounter self-taught graduates with uneven preparation and uncertainty about permissible uses.
qs: The lack of a coherent training approach among many law schools then shifts this obligation to legal employers.
Firms like Fredrikson & Byron
already are building AI fluency into associate development programs
The survey results suggest that what many law firms may be finding instead are graduates that are self-taught, inconsistently prepared, and uncertain about what they are permitted to do with AI.

kp.k: Employer AI access may influence graduate recruitment
kp.d: The narrative reports that absence of tools described as Fiduciary-Grade AI™ would influence role acceptance for 34% of students and 51% of heavy users. Figure 4 labels those shares “Possibly” on willingness to accept an offer without access, rather than outright refusal. The Institute predicts employer AI infrastructure will increasingly influence graduates’ choices. The document identifies Fiduciary-Grade AI™ as Thomson Reuters’ own standard, making this a branded survey framing rather than a generic tool category.
qs: While only 34% say the absence of Fiduciary-Grade AI™ tools would influence whether they accept a role, that number rises to 51% among heavy AI users.
As AI fluency becomes a more defining professional characteristic, prospective employers’ AI infrastructure will increasingly factor into where talented graduates choose to go.
At Thomson Reuters, Fiduciary‑Grade AI™ is our standard for how AI should work in high‑stakes professions.

kp.k: Educators face genuine governance, assessment, and judgment-development constraints
kp.d: The Institute acknowledges accreditation standards not designed for AI, faculty governance that slows curriculum change, and technology evolving faster than assessment frameworks. It also accepts the legitimacy of concerns about heavy early reliance impairing independent judgment. Its recommendation is structured integration with supervision, not unrestricted use or abandonment of foundational legal skills.
qs: law schools are navigating real tensions, including accreditation standards not written with AI in mind, faculty governance structures that make rapid curriculum change difficult, and a technology landscape that’s evolving faster than assessment frameworks can adapt.
There are also legitimate concerns about whether students who rely heavily on AI early in their education will develop the independent judgment the legal profession requires.
those concerns do not argue against structured AI integration, rather they argue for it.

kp.k: Law schools should integrate AI into curricula and assessment
kp.d: The Institute recommends replacing ad hoc faculty rules with institution-wide frameworks that classify permitted, encouraged, and prohibited uses, distinguish academic from clinical and professional contexts, and assess AI fluency alongside foundational skills. It frames AI as a core professional competency requiring structured supervision and ethical instruction, rather than an optional or peripheral educational issue.
qs: Legal educators should work to replace ad hoc faculty policies with institution-wide AI curriculum frameworks
assessment methods that evaluate whether students are developing AI fluency alongside the foundational skills that AI cannot replace.
treating AI as a core professional competency on par with others — a learned skill that requires structured supervision and ethically grounded instruction.

kp.k: Professional bodies should define and institutionalize AI competency
kp.d: The Institute treats ABA Formal Opinion 512 and Model Rules technology competency as starting foundations rather than sufficient responses. It recommends clearer AI competence obligations, integration into continuing legal education and admission processes, and accreditor consideration of what an AI-ready graduate should know. These are proposed changes, not reported requirements already adopted.
qs: ABA Formal Opinion 512, which establishes ethical guidance for lawyers using GenAI, can provide a good starting point, but it is not a finish line.
integrating AI competency into continuing legal education and admission processes
Accreditors should consider what an AI-ready graduate looks like and how law schools can meet the needs of a rapidly evolving practice ecosystem.

kp.k: Employers should publish AI expectations and communicate preparation gaps
kp.d: The Institute calls on law firms, corporate legal departments, and other legal organizations to make incoming-lawyer AI competency expectations public rather than confining them to onboarding. It argues that published expectations would create market pressure, provide schools with employer-defined curriculum targets, and give students transparent standards. Employers should also communicate candidly with schools about actual graduate skill levels.
qs: Firms should publish their AI competency expectations for incoming associates with the same visibility and accountability they bring to pro bono targets.
Published expectations create market pressure and give law schools a concrete, employer-defined target to build toward, as well as giving students a transparent standard to meet.
Firms should also be candid with law schools about what skill levels they are finding in the graduates they are hiring.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: The Institute presents AI literacy as an emerging professional competency and recruitment differentiator, while warning that automation of junior work may weaken the profession’s training pipeline.
pts.d: The Thomson Reuters Institute argues that widespread, largely self-directed student AI use is outpacing consistent institutional preparation. It reports that students regard AI as both professionally essential and a risk to foundational skill development. A quoted 1L describes intentional AI use as augmenting analysis rather than replacing critical thinking. The report argues that employers increasingly expect appropriate AI skills on arrival, shifting training obligations to employers when schools do not provide them. It reports student expectations of declining entry-level employment and warns that automating traditional junior assignments without replacement developmental pathways could create a future skills deficit. An anonymous student predicts junior redundancy rather than senior-lawyer replacement; a separate anonymous 2L predicts jobs managing AI associates and intervening in their mistakes. These are respondent predictions, not demonstrated employment outcomes. The Institute also predicts that employer AI infrastructure will increasingly influence graduate job choices. It argues that outright bans drive use underground and that supervised, ethically grounded integration is preferable to inconsistent restrictions.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence consists primarily of a student survey and qualitative responses, supplemented by employer anecdotes and a cited firm training example; the labour-market and skills-pipeline claims are expectations and conditional projections.
pts.d: The report draws on a web-based survey of 1,874 law students conducted April 6–19, 2026, including 1Ls (54%), 2Ls (26%), 3Ls (17%) and postgraduate students (3%), plus thematic analysis of 1,874 open-ended responses. It reports that 57% use AI for academic work several times weekly or more, rising to 84% among postgraduate students; 72% see learning AI as essential and 74% identify over-reliance risks. Institutional-gap findings include 48% reporting professor-specific policies, 15% no curriculum integration, and 32% disagreeing that school provides needed career AI skills. Forty-seven percent expect entry-level positions to decrease. For the next two to three years, students rate overall early-career impact at net −6 percentage points, independent judgment at −31, core skills at −14, mentorship and experiential learning each at −12, and creation of AI qualifications at +42. A student recounts a large-firm partner saying AI effectiveness had eliminated his practice group’s need to hire new associates for several years; this is a second-hand anecdote, not measured hiring data. Fredrikson & Byron is cited as integrating AI fluency into associate development, alongside anecdotal recruitment questions about AI use. The report interprets job-offer responses as indicating that access to tools influences 34% overall and 51% of heavy users; Figure 4 labels those shares 'Possibly' willing to accept an offer without the tools, rather than outright refusals. The question specifically concerns Thomson Reuters’ branded Fiduciary-Grade AI™ concept. No model-performance benchmark, longitudinal skills assessment or aggregate employer hiring series is offered for the displacement and development predictions.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The report describes an existing preparation gap in April 2026, records two-to-three-year student expectations, and projects longer-term training and recruitment consequences without fixed dates.
pts.d: Survey results describe respondents’ current experiences in April 2026. Figure 3 explicitly asks about AI’s impact on early-career professionals over the next two to three years. The skills-pipeline warning is conditional: harm follows if AI absorbs entry-level work without corresponding investment in alternative developmental pathways. The report suggests succession consequences could emerge 'in a few years' but provides no quantified timeline. The anonymous 2L’s prediction that AI will outperform associates at entry-level tasks is framed as inevitable 'at some point', not tied to a date. Increasing recruitment importance is conditional on AI fluency becoming a more defining professional characteristic. Benefits to learning are described as depending on intentional use, continued independent judgment, structured supervision and ethical guidance. The report acknowledges accreditation, faculty-governance and assessment constraints, and argues that guidance must differ across coursework, clinics, internships and practice.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The principal affected groups are law students and junior lawyers, their future senior colleagues, legal employers, and the institutions responsible for education and professional competency.
pts.d: Students face inconsistent permissions and uneven preparation while gaining opportunities to improve learning and differentiate themselves through AI fluency. Junior lawyers face possible reductions in traditional assignments and entry-level positions, alongside prospective work supervising AI. Future senior lawyers and firms face a conditional loss of accumulated expertise and succession capacity if foundational training is not replaced. Law firms, corporate legal departments and other legal organizations face incoming competency gaps, additional training responsibilities and possible recruitment disadvantages if they lack desired tools, especially among heavy student AI users. Law schools are urged to establish institution-wide frameworks and assess both AI fluency and independent foundational skills. Bar associations and accreditors are urged to clarify AI competency and integrate it into admission and continuing education. Client accuracy, trust, confidentiality and privilege feature as professional stakes, but the report does not measure client outcomes. Access to justice appears as a qualitative response theme rather than a developed or quantified prediction.
